verdicts.why: Making ready in advance is plain description; no attitude toward the thing prepared or the person preparing.
Cooking food is named without any judgement of it.
Drafting a speech or text is plain description of an act.
Having need of something states a fact and takes no side on it.
Requiring something as proper is plain modal statement; the word itself does not judge.
Feeling a need is neutral description of a state.
'Capable of X' states ability plainly; any approval belongs to the standalone 'a capable manager' sense, not this one.
'Capable of such an attempt' often pairs with bad objects, but the judgement lives in the object; the word merely states inclination.
Timing within a stage is plain description.
Before the expected time is a temporal fact, neither praised nor blamed by the word.
Being in good time is a temporal fact; any credit for punctuality is context, not a load the adverb carries.
Most recently is pure sequencing.
Being at the end of a sequence is plain ordering with no attitude.
Moving apart is described without judgement; 'they parted with the utmost politeness' shows the word carries none of its own.
Ending an association is a bad-ish referent named in a plain word; the word takes no side.
Departing is plain motion.
Getting over illness or shock is plain description of a change of state.
Getting something back is factual with no attitude toward the thing or the person.
Regaining or making up for is neutral description.
Quick and without warning is manner, not judgement; a strong meaning is not a loaded word.
Perceiving something is plain description.
Making a new finding is stated without attitude toward the finder or the finding.
Becoming aware of something is neutral; the word implies nothing about how the speaker feels about it.
Causing something to happen is plain causation.
Bringing an object out for display is plain description of an action.
